brief.subject: Diesel falls 16.5 cents; Mexico tariff threat returns
brief.headline: Diesel drops 16.5 cents as Trump threatens to double Mexico tariffs
brief.dek: Pump prices ease but stay above $6, a new tariff threat hits cross-border freight, and small-fleet capacity keeps shrinking.
brief.lede: The U.S. average for diesel fell 16.5 cents to $6.127 a gallon, but trade policy just got shakier for cross-border lanes.

sections.heading: Diesel eases but stays above $6
bullets: $6.127 per gallon: the national diesel average for the week of 2026-11-09, still a heavy weight on cost per mile.
Down 16.5 cents (2.6%) week over week, a modest break for carriers running tight margins.
Down 5.2 cents over four weeks, so relief is building slowly, not arriving all at once.
$6.23/gal at truck stops on Nov. 9, up 65% YoY even as Brent fell 21%, so refining margins are keeping pump prices high.

sections.heading: Tariff fight heats up again
bullets: Doubled Mexico tariffs are on the table unless the border migrant increase stops, a direct risk to cross-border freight volumes.
Democrats now control both chambers of Congress, adding uncertainty to the trade outlook and shipper planning.
Three bills in Congress would sharply limit presidential tariff power, and experts see possible bipartisan support.
Manufacturing advocates argue against rolling back trade enforcement, so expect a drawn-out policy fight.

sections.heading: Small-fleet tier keeps shrinking
bullets: About 362,000 tractors now run with one-to-six-truck carriers, down from a 2023 peak near 398,000.
Not all of that is failures; many trucks are moving elsewhere rather than leaving the industry.
15 bankruptcy filings and more than 1,000 job cuts in recent weeks show freight distress is ongoing.

sections.heading: Ocean imports cool from peak
bullets: Transpacific ocean rates eased slightly as U.S. port demand slows, though they remain elevated year over year.
Imports are coming off a near-record peak, which could thin out port drayage and import-driven loads.
Air cargo shows few signs of a late-year volume surge, hinting at a muted holiday freight finish.

sections.heading: Rail gains ground on intermodal
bullets: 6.6% year-over-year growth in U.S. rail traffic, led by intermodal, means more competition for long-haul truckload freight.
BLET ended its Wheeling & Lake Erie strike after winning protections for union conductors' work.
Genesee & Wyoming plans to split into three rail holding companies and sell dozens of short lines.
